strengths: Introduces semantic voting, a simple and computationally lightweight self-evaluation-free pseudo-labeling strategy that extends majority voting to open-ended tasks via soft semantic similarity.
The pipeline is practical: self-generation, clustering-based filtering, semantic voting, and DPO training are clearly specified and easy to implement.
The empirical study spans six LLMs and two open-ended task families, with lexical and semantic metrics, multiple ablations, hyperparameter analysis, an OOD evaluation, and a GRPO extension.

Efficiency analysis shows that constructing preference pairs with semantic voting is orders of magnitude cheaper than self-judging or entropy-minimization baselines, and does not scale with base model size.
The flipped-SV experiment is a useful sanity check against spurious reward signals and provides some evidence that the semantic voting signal is meaningful.
Reproducibility is relatively well supported through implementation details, prompt templates, and supplementary code/data.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: semantic voting is essentially average semantic self-consistency over sentence embeddings, combined with existing clustering and DPO components. The paper does not adequately position itself against prior semantic-consistency, semantic-entropy, or clustering-based pseudo-labeling work, and provides little theoretical justification for why average cosine similarity should reflect response quality.

The main evaluation appears transductive: the model is trained on the same unlabeled test inputs it is evaluated on. Although Appendix E reports some OOD transfer, gains are not universal, so the practical self-improvement/generalization claim is weaker than presented.

Baseline comparisons are not convincing. Self-judging and entropy minimization collapse catastrophically in many settings (e.g., EM on Llama-8B wmt24pp_de BLEU 0; SJ on Qwen-1.5B wmt24pp_de BLEU 3.45 vs. base 16.12), suggesting that the baselines may be poorly tuned or unfairly adapted to DPO. This undermines the central claim that SVSI outperforms self-evaluation methods.
Main DPO results lack variance estimates or multiple-seed reporting, so many reported gains may not be statistically reliable. The GRPO variant includes error bars, but the primary table does not.

Several datasets/models produce NA or zero-valid-output entries (e.g., Qwen-1.5B on pubmed; Qwen-3B on cnn_dailymail and pubmed), likely due to prompt, parsing, or truncation issues. These exclusions reduce coverage and reproducibility, but are not analyzed in depth.

The clustering/voting procedure has unresolved failure modes: there is no fallback when clustering yields no valid largest cluster or when the cluster has fewer than two responses, and discarding all but the largest cluster may throw away valid minority answers in high-diversity open-ended tasks.

The necessity and robustness of the clustering filter are not fully established: removing clustering sometimes improves performance (Qwen-1.5B), while the benefit for weaker models (Llama-1B) is used as post-hoc explanation rather than a principled criterion.

The efficiency claim is scoped to preference-pair construction time, not end-to-end self-improvement time. Since DPO training is shared across methods, the overall time savings may be smaller than the paper implies.

The framing of translation/summarization as 'unverifiable open-ended tasks' is somewhat overstated—translation can be evaluated with references, and the actual setting is better described as unsupervised test-time adaptation.

The empirical scope is narrow: only translation and summarization, with no evidence on reasoning, dialogue, instruction following, or other open-ended generation tasks where embedding-based semantic voting may behave differently.

strengths: The proposed method is simple and intuitive: it relaxes majority voting to soft semantic matching via sentence embeddings and constructs DPO preference pairs from high- and low-consensus answers.
The paper addresses a relevant and challenging problem: self-improvement on unverifiable open-ended tasks where exact-match majority voting is not directly applicable.
The experimental scope is reasonably broad, covering six models from Llama and Qwen families and multiple translation and summarization datasets.
The flipped-SV control experiment is a useful attempt to test whether the semantic voting signal is meaningful rather than a spurious reward.
The method has a clear efficiency motivation, and the paper includes some ablation and hyperparameter studies over embedding models, clustering algorithms, temperature, and sample size.
The reproducibility statement is promising, and the appendix provides implementation details, prompts, and hyperparameter settings.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: semantic voting is essentially a combination of self-consistency, sentence embedding similarity, clustering, and DPO. The core idea is simple and lacks theoretical grounding or a deeper analysis of why average cosine similarity should identify better responses.

The 'self-evaluation-free' claim is overstated. The method still relies on an external sentence embedding model as an evaluator, so it replaces LLM self-evaluation with embedding-model evaluation rather than eliminating evaluation.

The efficiency comparison is questionable. Entropy minimization can often be computed from logits during generation and should not require orders-of-magnitude more time than semantic voting. The reported 100x-1000x overhead for EM suggests an unfair or inefficient baseline implementation, which undermines the central efficiency claim.

Baseline results are highly unstable and in several places implausible. Self-judging and entropy minimization frequently collapse, produce zero BLEU/ROUGE scores, or are marked NA, raising concerns about prompt design, hyperparameter tuning, or implementation. These failures weaken the comparative evaluation.

Several settings are excluded because base models fail to produce valid outputs, and Qwen models show zero or NA results on summarization tasks. Such exclusions and anomalies make the evaluation appear cherry-picked or fragile, rather than providing a clean comparison.
The paper does not compare against other relevant self-improvement methods such as TTRL, ScPO, or other majority-voting-inspired or self-rewarding baselines, despite discussing them in related work.

SVSI does not consistently outperform baselines. EM or SJ is better in multiple settings, and the paper's own Figure 2 shows overlapping performance. The claim of overall better performance and greater stability is not fully supported.

The clustering step is a confound. Ablations show that removing clustering sometimes improves performance for Qwen-1.5B, and prior work such as EMPO already uses cluster-size signals. It is unclear how much of SVSI's gain comes from semantic voting versus clustering-based filtering.
The GRPO extension is weak and highly variable, with the authors themselves noting instability. It adds little evidence for the general extensibility of semantic voting.

There are no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals for the main table, making it difficult to judge whether the reported differences are meaningful. Hyperparameter studies are limited to a single dataset and may not generalize.

The evaluation metrics and protocol raise some concerns, including the use of reference-free or normalized metrics without sufficient justification and the lack of full-scale evaluation on standard summarization sets.

strengths: Proposes semantic voting, a simple and practical self-evaluation-free mechanism that generalizes majority voting to open-ended tasks via sentence-embedding similarity.
Integrates clustering-based filtering with semantic voting to construct DPO preference pairs, improving robustness to noisy self-generated candidates.
Conducts extensive experiments across 6 LLMs and multiple translation/summarization datasets, comparing against self-judging and entropy-minimization baselines.
Reports substantial efficiency gains in preference-pair construction and improved training stability relative to self-evaluation methods.
Includes thorough ablations on clustering, semantic voting, embedding models, clustering algorithms, and key hyperparameters.
Provides an out-of-distribution evaluation and a flipped-SV control experiment, strengthening confidence that the signal is meaningful rather than purely spurious.
Writing is clear, the algorithm is easy to follow, and implementation details plus code/data are provided for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is effectively transductive/test-time: the model is self-trained on the same unlabeled inputs used for evaluation, which can inflate in-domain gains and makes comparison with standard self-improvement settings less direct.

The efficiency advantage over entropy minimization is questionable: token- or trajectory-level entropy can often be computed from generation logits with little extra cost, so the reported orders-of-magnitude gap may be implementation-dependent or an unfair comparison.

Baseline results are sometimes catastrophic (e.g., BLEU 0, ROUGE 1.63), suggesting hyperparameter sensitivity or insufficient tuning; holding all training hyperparameters constant may disadvantage the self-evaluation baselines.

Main results are mixed: SVSI is not consistently better than entropy minimization, especially on Llama-3B translation and summarization, and the paper lacks variance estimates or statistical significance tests for many comparisons.
Novelty is moderate: semantic similarity and clustering for pseudo-labeling are natural extensions of existing self-consistency/majority-voting ideas, and the algorithm itself is relatively simple.
The method may reinforce systematic consensus errors or generic/fluent but incorrect outputs, and this failure mode is not deeply analyzed.
The GRPO-based extension shows substantial variance and is less stable than EMPO, weakening the claimed extensibility across training paradigms.
Some claims, such as 'consistently' outperforming self-evaluation methods, are stronger than the per-setting evidence supports.

strengths: Targets a relevant problem: self-improvement on open-ended unverifiable tasks without expensive self-evaluation.
Semantic voting is simple and computationally lightweight, using a sentence embedding model and average cosine similarity rather than additional LLM inference.
Empirical evaluation spans six base models and six datasets/tasks (translation and summarization), with comparisons to self-judging and entropy-minimization baselines.
Demonstrates large computational savings for preference-pair construction relative to self-evaluation baselines, and includes ablation, hyperparameter, and embedding-model sensitivity studies.
Includes flipped-SV and ranking-correlation analyses that provide some evidence that the semantic voting signal is not merely spurious.
Explores extensibility to GRPO and OOD/back-translation/instruction-following settings, improving the breadth of the empirical study.
The proposed clustering-filtering step is motivated and ablated, showing benefits especially for weaker models.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: semantic voting is essentially majority voting with cosine similarity plus clustering; the core mechanism is intuitive and incremental, not a fundamental advance.

Main results do not convincingly support the claim that the method consistently matches or surpasses self-evaluation baselines; on Llama-3B it is substantially worse than entropy minimization on many metrics.
No statistical significance tests or variance/error bars are reported for the main DPO experiments, so small differences and aggregate rankings may be noise.
The evaluation appears to use a test-time/transductive setup on the same inputs used for unsupervised tuning, rather than a clear held-out test split; this can overstate self-improvement.
Baselines may be under-tuned or brittle: entropy minimization and self-judging exhibit catastrophic failures on some models, making average comparisons and 'stability' claims less rigorous.
Some datasets/models are excluded due to base model failure to generate valid outputs, which may selectively remove unfavorable cases.
Reproducibility is weakened by missing/incomplete code release link, and important implementation details (seeds, exact data splits, significance) are absent.

The semantics of the pseudo-label are not directly validated; average semantic similarity can reward generic/modal responses and does not guarantee quality, and diversity/model-collapse issues are only briefly discussed.
The method is sensitive to clustering algorithm/hyperparameters and embedding model choice; no unified robust configuration is established, and conclusions vary across models.
The paper lacks human evaluation for open-ended generation quality, relying solely on automatic metrics; the 'unverifiable' claim is not fully tested with human judgments.

strengths: The paper targets a practically relevant problem: reducing the cost and bias of self-evaluation for LLM self-improvement on open-ended tasks.
The proposed method is simple, intuitive, and computationally efficient; using sentence embeddings for semantic voting avoids expensive LLM-as-a-judge or entropy-based scoring.
The efficiency claim is convincingly supported by Figure 3, showing orders-of-magnitude lower preference-pair construction time than SJ and EM.

The ablation and analysis sections are relatively thorough: flipped-SV validation, clustering ablation, embedding-model sensitivity, OOD/back-translation evaluation, diversity analysis, and Kendall-tau correlation with a reward model.
Implementation details, prompts, and training hyperparameters are largely provided, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: semantic voting is a straightforward soft-matching extension of majority voting using off-the-shelf sentence embeddings and clustering, combined with standard DPO. The paper does not engage sufficiently with prior work on semantic self-consistency, semantic entropy, or embedding-based consensus, and the core technical contribution is incremental.

The central empirical claim is overstated. Table 1 shows SVSI is not consistently better than EM or SJ; for example, EM substantially outperforms SVSI on Llama-3B translation, and several settings are mixed or marginal. The abstract’s claim of 'overall better performance' across diverse architectures and tasks is not well supported.

Main results lack statistical rigor: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests for DPO experiments. Given the reported instability in the GRPO variant and the sensitivity of DPO to noisy pairs, single-run comparisons are insufficient.

Evaluation is incomplete: several model/dataset combinations are NA or excluded due to base-model failures; summarization uses only 1,000 samples; the main paper evaluates only translation and summarization, with broader instruction-following and back-translation relegated to the appendix. No human evaluation is provided for open-ended quality.

Baselines are narrow: only SJ and EM (and EMPO/EMRL-seq for the GRPO variant) are compared. Relevant baselines such as clustering-based preference construction without voting, random preference pairs, semantic-entropy-style ranking, or other unsupervised preference-learning methods are missing or only partially ablated.

Method details and robustness are concerns. The similarity score divides by |A| rather than |A|-1, so it is not the stated average. Singleton or very small largest clusters are not handled, potentially producing invalid preference pairs. Clustering is fixed to HDBSCAN with limited sensitivity analysis, and the least-favored answer within the largest cluster may still be high quality, making the DPO negative noisy.

The parsing-based  oxed{} extraction may introduce selection bias: responses failing format constraints are discarded without reporting exclusion rates, and training DPO on parsed answers rather than full responses may lose reasoning behavior.

The paper observes reduced linguistic and semantic diversity after SVSI but dismisses it as unlikely to be serious. This is not adequately addressed; some apparent quality gains could be partly due to mode collapse or reduced output diversity rather than genuinely better semantic learning.
The released code link is absent in the manuscript, and the number of training runs, compute resources, and dataset sizes are not fully specified, limiting reproducibility.

Positioning is weak for a top-tier venue: efficiency is a clear positive, but the effectiveness evidence is mixed, the method is a simple combination of existing components, and the contribution does not yet meet the bar for a strong AI conference paper.

strengths: Proposes a simple, efficient, and intuitively motivated semantic voting mechanism that relaxes majority voting from exact matching to soft semantic similarity, avoiding expensive LLM self-evaluation.
Extensive empirical study across six base models, translation and summarization tasks, and multiple lexical/semantic metrics, with comparisons to self-judging and entropy-minimization baselines.
Demonstrates large computational savings for preference-pair construction (orders of magnitude lower than SJ/EM) and provides detailed implementation details, prompts, and released code.

Includes useful validation analyses: flipped-SV tests against spurious reward effects, clustering/SV ablations, embedding-model sensitivity, OOD evaluation, instruction-following, back-translation, linguistic-diversity, and ranking-correlation studies.
The method is broadly applicable in principle to other training paradigms, as shown by the GRPO-based SVSI-G variant, and is analyzed with appropriate caveats.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core idea combines existing components—majority voting, sentence embeddings, clustering-based filtering, and DPO—without substantial technical innovation or theoretical grounding.

Performance is not uniformly better than baselines: SVSI is weaker than EM on some summarization settings (e.g., Llama-3B) and occasionally below SJ or base models, so the claim of consistent superiority is overstated.

The approach relies on an external pretrained sentence embedding model, which somewhat undermines the 'self-evaluation-free' and self-contained framing; results also vary with embedding choice (e.g., DeBERTa-v3 on Llama-1B).

Clustering is not always beneficial; removing it can improve performance for Qwen-1.5B, and clustering may discard minority-but-valid responses, making the method sensitive to base-model capability and hyperparameters.
The GRPO variant is unstable due to continuous, high-cardinality rewards, and the paper only partly addresses instability via discretization in the appendix.
Efficiency comparisons focus on preference-pair construction time, while the full pipeline still requires sampling 64 responses per input, a shared and likely dominant cost not fully analyzed.
Several baseline comparisons are weakened by collapsed baselines (e.g., EM on Qwen-1.5B CNN/DailyMail, SJ yielding zeros), and excluded base-failure cases reduce the scope of the main table.

The theoretical justification for why average semantic similarity yields reliable preference signals is thin, and potential negative societal effects such as reduced diversity/model collapse are only briefly discussed.
